alalal-e80051-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 9: whether unformed faith becomes formed.

alalal-e80051-d1e113.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's text asking whether that unformed quality becomes formed.

alalal-e80051-d1e127.summary: Notes that Lombard says unformed faith becomes formed, but the masters disagree, so three questions will be pursued: whether unformed faith becomes formed; whether it is formed by its own form, by charity or by grace; and how these formations differ.

alalal-e80051-d1e161.summary: First argument that it is formed rather than replaced: nature does not destroy an unimpeded potency in a subject but perfects it; grace is no less ingenious, so arriving grace gives unformed faith only its tending to what is believed and does not destroy it.

alalal-e80051-d1e196.summary: Second argument: nature always takes the shortest path; grace even more so, and informing what exists is shorter than creating anew and then informing.

alalal-e80051-d1e220.summary: Third argument: everything unformed is formable unless the potency is corrupted, and the wayfarer remains capable of grace, so his faith is formable.

alalal-e80051-d1e240.summary: Fourth argument: unformed faith would be destroyed either by contrariety of its causes, as whiteness by heat, but both faiths come from God, or by contrariety to grace, but God's gifts and virtues are not contrary.

alalal-e80051-d1e273.summary: Fifth argument: gratuitously given grace is closer to sanctifying grace than natural or acquired virtue is, and grace does not destroy natural virtue but perfects it, so still less does it destroy unformed faith.

alalal-e80051-d1e295.summary: Further: grace does not destroy gratuitously given graces ordered to other acts, like wisdom or prophecy, so still less unformed faith, ordered to the same act.

alalal-e80051-d1e320.summary: Sixth argument: there is no conflict on the side of act and object, since believing God, believing that God is and believing into God are preserved; so the habit of unformed faith is preserved in formed faith.

alalal-e80051-d1e333.summary: Eighth argument: someone with formed faith who falls does not merit a new gift, so on restoration his faith is not newly infused, but only its form removed and restored.

alalal-e80051-d1e351.summary: Further: it would be ridiculous to receive a new faith at every fall, which would follow if the same faith could not become formed.

alalal-e80051-d1e364.summary: Rejects the reply that unformed faith is expelled as a lesser light by a greater: a lesser light joined to a greater is not destroyed, as sunbeams or candle-lights combine, and both faiths are the same kind of light by cause and object.

alalal-e80051-d1e390.summary: Ninth argument: if the sun could give light and heat separately, adding heat later would not remove the light but add to it; so first truth first gives light and later informs it by affect.

alalal-e80051-d1e412.summary: Contrary argument: sanctifying grace does the same in each person; in one with no faith it confers the fullness of all virtues, so it should do the same in one with unformed faith, not merely inform it.

alalal-e80051-d1e439.summary: Second contrary argument: a soul infused into a body with some prior operation would still be infused with all its powers, since it cannot be divided; grace, as the whole of the virtues, likewise gives all, and unformed faith, being superfluous, is expelled.

alalal-e80051-d1e472.summary: Third contrary argument: servile fear does not remain when charity arrives, since perfect charity casts out fear, so its cause, unformed faith, is also expelled.

alalal-e80051-d1e485.summary: Fourth contrary argument: a dead work is not revived when charity comes but perishes, and a new grace of working is given; so with dead faith.

alalal-e80051-d1e496.summary: Fifth contrary argument: 'formed faith is a virtue' is either per se, so the whole species is formed faith, or per accidens, which all deny.

alalal-e80051-d1e518.summary: Sixth contrary argument: two accidents do not make one accident unless as genus and difference; unformed and formed faith are both habits, so they do not make one habit.

alalal-e80051-d1e538.summary: Solution: with Lombard, unformed faith becomes formed through arriving grace and charity, so the first arguments are to be granted.
claims: Unformed faith itself becomes formed by the arrival of grace and charity.

alalal-e80051-d1e555.summary: Reply to the first contrary argument: grace of itself does the same in all, but varies by the subject: it perfects natural virtues where present, removes sin where present, informs unformed faith where present, and infuses whole faith where absent, from the subject's disposition, not its own defect.
claims: Grace acts differently according to the subject's prior state, informing faith that is present and infusing it where absent.

alalal-e80051-d1e586.summary: Reply to the soul analogy: a soul would be infused whole because a prior bodily power is rooted in the body's complexion and cannot unite with the spiritual; but unformed and formed faith come from the same efficient cause, God, and so are unitable.
concepts: unitability of habits from the same cause

alalal-e80051-d1e615.summary: Reply on servile fear: fear is not removed as fear but as servile; so the unformedness of faith is removed, not faith, just as in heaven faith's substance remains as vision of truth, while its form of seeing in a mirror and enigma passes.
claims: Charity removes the unformedness of faith, not faith itself, as it removes the servility of fear, not fear.

alalal-e80051-d1e641.summary: Reply on dead works: dead works come not from a living cause but from free choice lying dead in sins, while faith comes from first truth, which cannot die; faith dies not in itself but from another's defect.

alalal-e80051-d1e659.summary: Reply on predication: 'formed faith is a virtue' is per se predication of the perfect species of virtue; 'unformed faith is a virtue' is predication by posteriority.

alalal-e80051-d1e679.summary: Reply on unity of accidents: the principle is false in rational and natural things; dispositions of acts combine into one habit, and light at the edge of a transparent body becomes one with colour. One is always as potency and the other as act; so unformed faith is as potency and formed faith as its act, enabling it to tend to and unite with the end.
claims: Unformed faith is to formed faith as potency to act, forming one habit.

alalal-e80051-d1e724.summary: Since many great masters hold the opposite view, Albert gives replies on their behalf. To the first argument: nature and grace differ, since natural powers are rooted in diverse principles and survive, while in grace all virtues exist in one virtual whole, grace, and are given or removed together because of grace's perfection and the connection of virtues.

alalal-e80051-d1e761.summary: For the opposing view, to the second argument: the shortest way of justification is to infuse the whole at once and remove what does not justify.

alalal-e80051-d1e772.summary: For the opposing view, to the third: unformed virtue is so called not because formable but from privation of the form, grace, and of potency to it; the impediment is its imperfection, which makes it unitable with perfect grace, as a fire's ray is not united with the sun's but extinguished.

alalal-e80051-d1e796.summary: For the opposing view, to the fourth: unformed faith is destroyed as not unitable with grace, as sunlight excludes firelight from the same recipient; though some of this view say it remains, not superfluously, making the intellect pass more easily into the act of believing.

alalal-e80051-d1e820.summary: For the opposing view, to the next arguments: some say natural virtues remain with gratuitous ones, others that they are absorbed because of imperfection, as two qualities of the same species in a body succeed by absorption.

alalal-e80051-d1e840.summary: For the opposing view, to the sixth: though there is no conflict of act or object, one is imperfect and cannot stand with the perfect light; or, as others say, it remains, differently ordered, unformed faith believing God and that God is, formed faith believing into God.

alalal-e80051-d1e861.summary: For the opposing view, to the eighth: it is not absurd for the habit of unformed faith to be created at each fall, not because the sinner merits it, but because God in his mercy gives even the wicked the means to return; or, as others say, it stays the same and is not removed by sin.

alalal-e80051-d1e885.summary: For the opposing view, to the light argument: unformed faith is not wholly equivocal with formed faith, so it can be expelled by it; or, as others say, both remain.

alalal-e80051-d1e898.summary: For the opposing view, to the last: sunlight and heat are divisible in effect, but grace and faith are not; grace gives virtue only by giving the whole, needing nothing else, and so expels what is imperfect; or it may be granted that it remains.

alalal-e80051-d1e922.summary: Concludes that, though such replies are possible, the replies themselves show that the first opinion, that unformed faith becomes formed, is sounder.
claims: The view that unformed faith is itself formed is sounder than the view that it is replaced.

alalal-e80051.summary: Article 9 takes up the disputed question whether unformed faith itself becomes formed when grace and charity arrive, or is expelled and replaced. Arguments for formation appeal to grace perfecting rather than destroying, to its economy, to the absence of contrariety among God's gifts, and to the absurdity of receiving a new faith at every fall. Arguments for replacement appeal to grace's uniform action, its giving all virtues as a whole, charity's casting out of fear, and the unity of habits. With Lombard, Albert holds that unformed faith becomes formed. Grace varies its effect by the subject's prior state. The two faiths come from the same cause and can unite as potency and act. Charity removes the unformedness, as it removes the servility of fear, not faith itself. Faith, coming from first truth, dies only through another's defect. He sets out how the opposing masters could answer, citing the connection of virtues in grace and the imperfection of unformed faith, but judges his own view the sounder.
claims: Unformed faith itself becomes formed when grace and charity arrive; it is not replaced.
Grace acts according to the subject's prior state, informing faith where it exists and infusing it where it does not.
Charity removes the unformedness of faith, not faith itself, as it removes servility, not fear.
Unformed and formed faith relate as potency and act within one habit.
